title: 1 Kings 17:17–24
context: The widow’s son falls so ill that no breath is left in him, and in her grief she asks whether Elijah has come to bring her sin to remembrance and kill her son. Elijah carries the boy to his upper room, cries out to the LORD, stretches himself on the child three times, and the LORD hears him, so that the child’s life returns. The widow confesses that Elijah is a man of God and that the LORD’s word in his mouth is truth. Hebrews 11:35 speaks of women who received their dead by resurrection, which interpreters commonly connect with this account and the similar one in Elisha’s ministry. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about the LORD who rules over life and death, hears prayer, and meets a grieving outsider with mercy.

verses.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became sick; and his sickness was so severe that there was no breath left in him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the widow’s son becoming so sick that no breath is left in him. Even after provision, sorrow comes into the household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the illness as a hard providence that will reveal God’s power over life. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sympathy for the grieving mother.

verses.text: She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the widow asking whether Elijah has come to bring her sin to memory and kill her son. Grief and guilt mingle in her words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her question as an honest cry from a troubled conscience. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how suffering can stir fear of judgment, without the text saying her sin caused the death.

verses.text: He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah asking for the boy and carrying him to his own room. He takes the burden on himself and brings it to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s action as compassionate and purposeful. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the prophet bringing the need directly before God.

verses.text: He cried to the LORD and said, “LORD my God, have you also brought evil on the widow with whom I am staying, by killing her son?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah crying to the LORD and asking whether he has brought evil on the widow. His prayer is honest and even bewildered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah wrestling with God’s providence in prayer. Both traditions commonly value the verse as permission to bring painful questions to God.

verses.text: He stretched himself on the child three times, and cried to the LORD and said, “LORD my God, please let this child’s soul come into him again.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah stretching himself on the child three times and pleading for the child’s soul to return. His prayer is persistent and earnest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s action and prayer as means God uses to display his power. Readers in both traditions commonly hold that the life comes from the LORD, not from the gesture itself.

verses.text: The LORD listened to the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD listening to Elijah’s voice and the child reviving. God responds to the prayer of his servant (compare James 5:17–18).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who gives life to the dead (compare Romans 4:17). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sign of God’s power over death.

verses.text: Elijah took the child and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah bringing the child down and giving him to his mother, saying your son lives. Joy replaces grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo in Jesus giving a raised son back to his mother at Nain (Luke 7:15). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of God’s compassion.

verses.text: The woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the LORD’s word in your mouth is truth.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the widow confessing that Elijah is a man of God and that the LORD’s word in his mouth is truth. Faith grows through experience of God’s power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her confession as recognition of the true God by a Gentile. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the climax of the chapter: the LORD’s word is truth.
